questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Clearing of a competitive labor market
questions.learningObjective: Identify the market-clearing wage where labor supply equals demand
questions.stem: A software team posts a ticket for 40 backend roles at a wage where applicants exactly match openings.

options.text: The wage clears the market with no persistent shortage or surplus
The wage is above equilibrium and creates a surplus of applicants
options.misconception: confuses a shortage with a surplus of labor

options.text: The wage must fall because employers always prefer lower pay
options.misconception: assumes employer preference alone sets wages

options.text: The wage creates unemployment because too many workers apply
options.misconception: treats any applicant pool as unemployment

questions.explanation: At the equilibrium wage, quantity of labor supplied equals quantity demanded, so there is no shortage or surplus. A higher wage would create surplus applicants, while a lower wage would leave openings unfilled.
questions.hint: Look for equality of supplied and demanded labor.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Recognize monopsony from a single buyer with MFC above the wage
questions.stem: A ticket notes one buyer of labor where MRP equals MFC at 12 workers while the wage is 30 and MFC is 45.

options.text: Employment is competitive because MRP equals MFC at 12
options.misconception: ignores that MFC exceeds wage in monopsony

options.text: The wage equals MFC so workers are paid their marginal product
options.misconception: confuses marginal factor cost with wage

options.text: The monopsonist hires fewer workers than a competitive market would
A higher wage would reduce employment in this market

questions.explanation: In monopsony, MFC lies above the supply wage, so MRP equals MFC at a lower employment level than where MRP equals wage. The gap between MFC and wage shows market power.
questions.hint: Compare MFC with the supply wage.

questions.explanation: MFC equals 10 + 2L, so setting 100 - 2L = 10 + 2L gives 90 = 4L and L = 22.5. The monopsonist stops where marginal cost meets marginal revenue product.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why MFC exceeds the wage
questions.stem: Explain why marginal factor cost exceeds the wage in a monopsonistic labor market.

answer.exemplar: Marginal factor cost exceeds the wage because hiring an extra worker raises the wage for all existing workers, so the extra cost includes both the new worker's wage and the raise paid to everyone already employed.

questions.explanation: The supply curve gives the wage for each employment level, and moving along it raises pay for all workers. Therefore the marginal cost of labor includes the inframarginal wage increase.
questions.hint: Account for the raise to existing workers.

questions.stem: A ticket records MRP 80 and wage 50 for a monopsonist's last hired worker.

options.text: There is no exploitation if MRP exceeds the wage
options.misconception: denies exploitation whenever MRP exceeds wage

options.text: Exploitation is 50 because that is the wage paid
options.misconception: identifies the wage itself as exploitation

options.text: Exploitation is 80 because that is marginal revenue product
options.misconception: confuses total product with the gap

options.text: Exploitation is 30, the gap between MRP and the wage

questions.explanation: Monopsony exploitation is the difference between what a worker produces at the margin and what the worker is paid. Here that difference is 80 minus 50, or 30.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why a monopsonist chooses employment where MRP equals MFC rather than where MRP equals wage.

answer.exemplar: A monopsonist maximizes profit by hiring until the cost of the last worker equals the revenue that worker generates, and because MFC exceeds wage, that equality occurs at a lower employment level than MRP equals wage.

questions.explanation: Profit maximization requires marginal cost to equal marginal revenue. In monopsony marginal cost is MFC, not wage, so the stopping rule uses MFC.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Clearing of a competitive labor market
questions.stem: What does it mean for a competitive labor market to clear?

answer.exemplar: A competitive labor market clears when the wage adjusts so that the quantity of labor workers are willing to supply equals the quantity employers want to hire, leaving no persistent shortage or surplus.

questions.explanation: Market clearing is an equality condition, not a statement about any single employer. If supply and demand differ, wage pressure moves the market toward equality.
questions.hint: Set supplied labor equal to demanded labor.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain the wedge between MFC and wage in monopsony.

answer.exemplar: The wedge arises because the supply curve is upward sloping: to hire another worker the monopsonist must raise the wage for all workers, so marginal factor cost includes both the new wage and the raise to existing workers.

questions.explanation: The wedge is not a tax; it is the cost of moving up the supply curve. It shrinks only if supply becomes more elastic.
questions.hint: Think cost of raising all wages.

questions.stem: Explain how a monopsonist chooses employment using MRP and MFC.

answer.exemplar: A monopsonist increases employment as long as MRP exceeds MFC and stops where MRP equals MFC, because beyond that point an extra worker costs more than the revenue generated.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why marginal factor cost exceeds wage when labor supply slopes upward.

answer.exemplar: Marginal factor cost exceeds wage because hiring an additional worker requires raising the wage for all workers, so the marginal cost includes the new worker's wage plus the raise paid to existing workers.

questions.explanation: The supply curve determines both wage and MFC. An upward slope makes the marginal cost of labor greater than its price.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why a monopsonist stops hiring where MRP equals MFC.

answer.exemplar: A monopsonist stops where MRP equals MFC because beyond that point the cost of an additional worker exceeds the revenue that worker generates, reducing profit.

questions.explanation: Marginal decision-making requires comparing marginal revenue with marginal cost. In monopsony the relevant cost is MFC.
questions.hint: Compare marginal revenue and marginal cost.
